clue.text: A case of simultaneous hit and run

definitions.text: A case of simultaneous hit and run

parts.words: A case of simultaneous hit and run
parts.note: surface reading: a road accident where a driver strikes someone and flees at once
setter's reading: the ancient horse-archers of Parthia fired arrows back at the enemy while riding away

explanation.surface: A motoring offence in which the driver strikes someone and speeds off in the same moment.
explanation.walkthrough: The Parthians were mounted archers who shot backwards while retreating, so their arrow lands as they run; the phrase now means a cutting remark made on leaving.
explanation.definitionFit: The archers of ancient Parthia struck their enemy while retreating, literally hitting and fleeing at once.

clue.text: A shady put-up job

parts.note: surface reading: a dishonest scheme arranged in advance to deceive someone
setter's reading: something that gives shade and is opened up over the head

explanation.surface: A crooked swindle rigged in advance by dubious characters.
explanation.walkthrough: Shady and put-up job both suggest crime, but here shady means casting shade and put-up means raised overhead.
explanation.definitionFit: A sunshade is an object raised above the head on a stick to cast shade, a literal shady put-up thing.

clue.text: Some interest perhaps concerning the meeting-place

parts.note: re is the Latin-derived word for about or concerning
a venue is where an event or meeting is held

explanation.surface: A note on how the people at a gathering feel about the place they meet.
explanation.walkthrough: Interest here is money earned on savings, not curiosity; the 'perhaps' warns that it is only one kind of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Revenue is income of any kind, and interest earned on capital is one example of it.

clue.text: Burnt offering arranged at upper-class school

indicators.note: things that are arranged are put into a new order, so the letters that follow are reordered

parts.note: taken as written
U is the classic abbreviation for upper-class
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sacrificial rite staged at a posh public school.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class comes from the 1950s debate on 'U and non-U' speech, and crosswords use it constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: The word's original sense is a sacrifice wholly consumed by fire, from Greek for 'burnt whole'.

clue.text: Tree one in a hundred with some eminence

parts.note: a means one, as in a single thing
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
a tor is a rocky hill, a piece of high ground or eminence

explanation.surface: A tree that stands out from a hundred others by growing on high ground.
explanation.walkthrough: Tree is not a plant: Sir Herbert Beerbohm Tree was a famous Victorian stage star and theatre manager. The surface also flatters him as one in a hundred.
explanation.definitionFit: Herbert Beerbohm Tree was a celebrated English stage performer, so he is an example of a player.

clue.text: No conscientious reader, the master

definitions.meaning: first meaning: someone who skips pages while reading
second meaning: the captain of a ship

explanation.surface: A complaint that the schoolmaster does not read his pupils' work carefully.
explanation.definitionFit: One who jumps over passages is a careless reader, and the same word is the everyday name for a ship's captain.

clue.text: Beaten away, finished

parts.note: someone who is away is out
something finished is done

explanation.surface: A sports report: the side was defeated in an away match and is now out of the competition.
explanation.definitionFit: To be outdone is to be surpassed or bettered by a rival, so defeated.

clue.text: Madam let a car crash into this animal

indicators.note: a crash smashes things up, so the words before it are broken and rebuilt

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A careless lady driver lets her car run into a stray animal.
explanation.walkthrough: The animal in the surface is the victim of the accident; the twelve letters of the first four words make it.
explanation.definitionFit: A ginger tabby is commonly called by this name after the orange colour of the preserve.

clue.text: A Sheridan character, we hear, is coming

indicators.note: what we hear is the spoken form, so the sound counts and not the spelling

parts.note: Sheridan wrote the comedy The Rivals, so any of its characters is a rival

explanation.surface: An announcement that a figure from a Sheridan play is about to appear on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Brinsley Sheridan's best-known play is The Rivals (1775), so one of its cast is a rival.
explanation.definitionFit: Coming as a noun means an approach or appearance, which is what an arrival is.

clue.text: His love is no end older

definitions.text: His love is no end older

parts.words: His love is no end older
parts.note: surface reading: someone's beloved is getting very much older
setter's reading: the word is followed by older without its last letter, which spells the lover's name

explanation.surface: A man notices his sweetheart has aged enormously.
explanation.walkthrough: IS plus OLDE(R) spells ISOLDE, and the knight whose love she was is the answer. 'No end' looks like 'hugely' but means drop the final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Arthurian legend the knight of Cornwall fell fatally in love with the Irish princess Isolde.

clue.text: Settlers, naturally — but not of tailors' bills

definitions.text: Settlers, naturally — but not of tailors' bills

parts.note: surface reading: of course these are colonists who have settled somewhere

parts.words: naturally — but not of tailors' bills
parts.note: setter's reading: they live in the natural state and so never settle a bill for clothes

explanation.surface: Colonists who, of course, never pay what they owe their tailors.
explanation.walkthrough: Settlers means both colonists and those who settle bills; naturally hints at going unclothed, so no tailor is ever paid.
explanation.definitionFit: A community of naturists living together without clothing is a settlement whose members never buy suits.

clue.text: Monica's crafty

indicators.note: crafty suggests cunning work, so the name is skilfully reworked into new order

parts.note: the name with its possessive s, taken as written

explanation.surface: A remark that a woman called Monica is sly.
explanation.walkthrough: Crafty does double duty: it tells you to rework the name and defines the answer, since Freemasons call their movement the Craft.
explanation.definitionFit: Freemasonry is known to its members as the Craft, so anything belonging to it is jokingly crafty.

clue.text: Copper and gold invested in free insurance for sky-divers

indicators.note: money invested in something is put inside it, so these go within the outer word

parts.note: to free someone of a thing is to rid them of it
a copper is a policeman, a PC or police constable
or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: Metal holdings put into a free-cover policy for parachutists.
explanation.walkthrough: Copper and gold look like metals in an investment portfolio, but copper is a police officer here, and the heraldic word stands for gold.
explanation.definitionFit: The cord pulled to open a parachute is what keeps a jumper safe, a lifeline in place of a policy.

clue.text: Many coming to that Roman city in France

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty, crossword shorthand for many
ille is the Latin word for that

explanation.surface: Crowds of people visiting a French city that was once Roman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roman' is not historical colour: it says to put 'that' into Latin.
explanation.definitionFit: Lille is a large industrial city in the far north of the country, near the Belgian border.

clue.text: Those who do so should remove all traces, etc

definitions.text: Those who do so should remove all traces, etc

parts.note: surface reading: people who leave no evidence behind, like criminals cleaning up
setter's reading: traces are the side straps by which a horse pulls a cart, and the etc covers the rest of its tack

explanation.surface: Advice that anyone doing this job must leave no evidence behind.
explanation.walkthrough: Traces suggest clues at a crime scene, but they are the straps linking a draught horse to its load.
explanation.definitionFit: To free a horse from its tack is to take off the traces, collar, bridle and other straps.

clue.text: Maybe either state is unorthodox

indicators.note: maybe means the letters are only one possibility, so they may take another arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
Cal is a short form for California, a US state

explanation.surface: A suggestion that holding both views at once is unconventional.
explanation.walkthrough: Either is shuffled, then CAL, a short form for California, is added.
explanation.definitionFit: A heretical view departs from accepted church doctrine, the very opposite of orthodox belief.

clue.text: An emendator? A Welsher, rather

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read cryptically: one who takes the faults out of a text
second meaning: someone who fails to pay a debt, especially a bet

explanation.surface: Someone asking whether a textual corrector is really just a cheat.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the first meaning as a pun: de- plus faulter, one who removes faults. To welsh is to dodge paying a betting debt.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who fails to meet a payment obligation is said to have defaulted, exactly what a welsher does.

clue.text: After a month anger becomes feverish

parts.note: Feb is the abbreviation for February
to rile is to anger

explanation.surface: After a month of tension, someone's anger turns into agitation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' sets the order: the month comes first and the anger follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: Febrile is the medical adjective for having a fever, and figuratively for hectic excitement.

clue.text: Pack-drill? Not for such a one

definitions.text: Pack-drill? Not for such a one

parts.words: Pack-drill? Not for such a one
parts.note: surface reading: some soldier is spared a punishment march with full kit
setter's reading: the old army saying no names, no pack-drill, meaning that whoever is not identified cannot be punished

explanation.surface: A sergeant deciding that one particular soldier will escape punishment drill.
explanation.walkthrough: Pack-drill was a military punishment of marching in full kit; the proverb says that if nobody is named, nobody is punished.
explanation.definitionFit: A person never identified escapes blame, since in the old army saying punishment needs a name.

clue.text: Sharp girl's given a start by this instrument

parts.note: surface reading: a quick-witted girl is startled

parts.words: Sharp girl's given a start by this instrument
parts.note: setter's reading: Thackeray's Becky Sharp was christened with a longer name, and the instrument's name forms its opening five letters

explanation.surface: A clever girl jumps at the sound of a musical instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: Becky Sharp is the heroine of Thackeray's Vanity Fair, christened Rebecca; the answer supplies the start of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: The rebec is a medieval bowed string instrument, an early relative of the fiddle.

clue.text: Call about a member doing a swindle

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the outer word wraps round what follows

parts.note: to ring is to call on the telephone
taken as written
MP, Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A phone call concerning an MP mixed up in a fraud.
explanation.walkthrough: Member is the usual crossword shorthand for a Member of Parliament. A ramp is old British slang for a swindle or racket.
explanation.definitionFit: Ramping is British slang for running a racket, especially pushing prices up dishonestly.

clue.text: Scholar right to admit one in the Ruddigore gallery

parts.note: a BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a graduate scholar

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so the pair before it opens to hold what follows

parts.note: rt is an abbreviation for right
taken as written

explanation.surface: A scholar is entitled to admit someone to the opera's picture gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: In Gilbert and Sullivan's Ruddigore, the portraits of the dead Baronets of Ruddigore come to life and step out of their frames. 'One' serves both the wordplay and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The ghostly ancestors in the portrait gallery of the Gilbert and Sullivan opera are all holders of that hereditary title.

clue.text: Transport I catch to this meeting of governors

parts.note: a cab is a means of transport, a taxi
taken as written
to net is to catch

explanation.surface: Someone explains they catch a ride to an important board meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: The senior ministers who run a country meet as a body, and that group of rulers is so named.

clue.text: Go round Piedmont's second — no, first — city

indicators.note: going round something encloses it, so the outer word wraps the chosen letter

parts.note: a go or a turn is a player's chance to play

indicators.note: second points to the letter in the second position of the place name

parts.note: the region's name supplies only one letter

explanation.surface: A tourist's directions to circle a city that is Piedmont's second, then corrected to its first.
explanation.walkthrough: The aside 'no, first' looks like a correction to the wordplay; it is part of the definition, since this is Piedmont's chief city.
explanation.definitionFit: Turin is the capital and largest city of the Piedmont region in north-west Italy.

clue.text: Sound quality? Pound the old tambourine

parts.note: timbre is the tone colour of a sound
L is the abbreviation for a pound sterling, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: A question about tone, then an order to beat an old tambourine.
explanation.walkthrough: Pound looks like a verb for beating the drum, but it is the money.
explanation.definitionFit: Timbrel is the archaic and biblical word for a small hand drum or tambourine.

clue.text: Comparatively spruce, the Vicar of Bray

definitions.meaning: first meaning: neater, the comparative of trim
second meaning: one who changes opinions to suit whoever is in power

explanation.walkthrough: The Vicar of Bray, in an English folk song, keeps his parish by switching his religion with every new monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Neater is the comparative of trim, and a political turncoat who shifts with the times is called by the same word.

clue.text: It looks grand in feature on hair-style

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another, so the facial word holds the letter before it

parts.note: a chin is a feature of the face
G is short for grand, a thousand pounds or dollars
taken as written

explanation.surface: Admiring a new hair-do that looks grand in a magazine feature.
explanation.walkthrough: Feature looks like a magazine article but is part of the face. 'It looks' just introduces the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A chignon is a knot or roll of hair worn at the nape of the neck, a classic hair arrangement.

clue.text: Important man's link with the Star of Bethlehem?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a prominent figure in some field
second meaning, read literally: the star that guided the wise men to the manger

explanation.surface: A question about some great man's connection with the Nativity star.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the literal sense: the star led the Magi, so it was a light that did the leading.
explanation.definitionFit: A prominent person is idiomatically called this, and the Nativity star literally guided travellers to Bethlehem.
